section.heading: 9.4 Duality
section.paragraph: Associated with each canonical (maximization) linear programming problem is a related minimization problem, called the dual problem. In this setting, the canonical problem is called the primal problem. This section describes the dual problem and how it is solved, along with an interesting economic interpretation of the dual variables. The section concludes by showing how any matrix game can be solved using the primal and dual versions of a suitable linear programming problem.

Given vectors $$\mathbf{c}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ and $$\mathbf{b}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ , and given an $$m \times n$$ matrix $$A$$ , the canonical (primal) problem is to find $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ so as to maximize $$f(\textbf{x}) = \textbf{c}^{T}\textbf{x}$$ subject to the constraints $$A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$$ and $$\textbf{x} \geq \textbf{0}$$ . The dual (minimization) problem is to find $$\mathbf{y}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ so as to minimize $$g(\textbf{y}) = \textbf{b}^{T}\textbf{y}$$ subject to $$A^{T}\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{c}$$ and $$\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{0}$$ :

image.alt: A table lists three constraints each for primal problem P and dual problem P asterisk.

section.paragraph: Observe that in forming the dual problem, the $$c_{i}$$ coefficients of $$x_{i}$$ in the objective function of the primal problem become the constants on the right-hand side of the constraint inequalities in the dual. Likewise, the numbers in the right-hand side of the constraint inequalities in the primal problem become the coefficients $$b_{j}$$ of $$y_{j}$$ in the objective function in the dual. Also, note that the direction of the constraint inequalities is reversed from $$A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$$ to $$A^{T}\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{c}$$ . In both cases, the variables $$\mathbf{x}$$ and $$\mathbf{y}$$ are nonnegative.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Find the dual of the following primal problem:

$$\begin{matrix} \text{Maximize} & 5 x_{1} + 7 x_{2} & & \\ \text{subject} \text{to} & 2 x_{1} + 3 x_{2} & \leq & 25 \\ & 7 x_{1} + 4 x_{2} & \leq & 16 \\ & x_{1} + 9 x_{2} & \leq & 21\end{matrix} \text{and} x_{1} \geq 0 , x_{2} \geq 0.$$
example.heading: Solution

section.paragraph: Suppose that the dual problem above is rewritten as a canonical maximization problem:
$$\text{Maximize} & h \left(\textbf{y}\right) = - \textbf{b}^{T} \textbf{y} \text{subject to} & - A^{T} \textbf{y} \leq - \textbf{c} \text{and} \textbf{y} \geq \textbf{0} .$$
Then the dual of this problem is

$$\text{Maximize} & F \left(\textbf{w}\right) = - \textbf{c}^{T} \textbf{w} \text{subject to} & \left(\right. - A^{T} \left.\right)^{T} \textbf{w} \geq - \textbf{b} \text{and} \textbf{w} \geq \textbf{0} .$$
In canonical form, this minimization problem is equivalent to
$$\text{Maximize} & G \left(\textbf{w}\right) = \textbf{c}^{T} \textbf{w} \text{subject to} & A \textbf{w} \leq \textbf{b} \text{and} \textbf{w} \geq \textbf{0} .$$
If $$\mathbf{w}$$ is replaced by $$\mathbf{x}$$ , this problem is precisely the primal problem. So the dual of the dual problem is the original primal problem.
Theorem 7 below is a fundamental result in linear programming. As with the Minimax Theorem in game theory, the proof depends on certain properties of convex sets and hyperplanes.1

note.title: Theorem ﻿7
note.heading: Theorem ﻿7
The Duality Theorem﻿
note.paragraph: Let $$P$$ be a (primal) linear programming problem with feasible set $$\mathcal{F}$$ , and let $$P^{\ast}$$ be the dual problem with feasible set $$\mathcal{F}^{\ast}$$ .

list.item: If $$\mathcal{F}$$ and $$\mathcal{F}^{\ast}$$ are both nonempty, then $$P$$ and $$P^{\ast}$$ both have optimal solutions, say $$\mathbf{\overline{x}}$$ and $$\mathbf{\overline{y}}$$ , respectively, and $$f(\mathbf{\overline{x}}) = g(\mathbf{\overline{y}})$$ .

If one of the problems $$P$$ or $$P^{\ast}$$ has an optimal solution $$\mathbf{\overline{x}}$$ or $$\mathbf{\overline{y}}$$ , respectively, then so does the other, and $$f(\mathbf{\overline{x}}) = g(\mathbf{\overline{y}})$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Set up and solve the dual to the problem in Example 5 of Section 9.2.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The original problem is to

$$\begin{matrix} \text{Maximize} & f ( x_{1} , x_{2} ) & = & 2 x_{1} + 3 x_{2} \\ \text{subject to} & x_{1} & \leq & 30 \\ & x_{2} & \leq & 20 \\ & x_{1} + 2 x_{2} & \leq & 54\end{matrix} \text{and} x_{1} \geq 0 , x_{2} \geq 0.$$

Calculations in Example 5 of Section 9.2 showed that the optimal solution of this problem is $$\mathbf{\overline{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} 30 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix}$$ with $$f(\mathbf{\overline{x}}) = 96$$ . The dual problem is to

$$\begin{matrix} \text{Minimize} & g \left(y_{1} , y_{2} , y_{3}\right) & = & 30 y_{1} + 20 y_{2} + 54 y_{3} \\ \text{subject to} & \textit{y}_{ \text{1} } + y_{3} & \geq & 2 \\ & y_{2} + 2 y_{3} & \geq & 3\end{matrix} \text{and} y_{1} \geq 0 , y_{2} \geq 0 , y_{3} \geq 0.$$

The simplex method could be used here, but the geometric method of Section 9.2 is not too difficult. Graphs of the constraint inequalities (Figure 1) reveal that $$\mathcal{F}^{\ast}$$ has three extreme points and that $$\overline{\mathbf{y}} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{3}{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ is the optimal solution. Indeed, $$g(\overline{\mathbf{y}}) = 30\left( \frac{1}{2} \right) + 20(0) + 54\left( \frac{3}{2} \right) = 96,$$ as expected.

image.alt: An illustration of the geometric method to find the minimum is provided, along with a table containing the data for y and g (y).

section.paragraph: Notice that the optimal solution to the dual problem appears in the bottom row. The variables $$x_{3}$$ , $$x_{4}$$ , and $$x_{5}$$ are the slack variables for the first, second, and third equations, respectively. The bottom entry in each of these columns gives the optimal solution $$\overline{\mathbf{y}} = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{l} \frac{1}{2} \\ 0 \\ \frac{3}{2} \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ to the dual problem. note.title: Theorem ﻿7
note.heading: Theorem ﻿7
The Duality Theorem﻿ (continued)
note.paragraph: Let $$P$$ be a (primal) linear programming problem and let $$P^{\ast}$$ be its dual problem. Suppose $$P$$ (or $$P^{\ast}$$ ) has an optimal solution.

list.item: If either $$P$$ or $$P^{\ast}$$ is solved by the simplex method, then the solution of its dual is displayed in the bottom row of the final tableau in the columns associated with the slack variables.

section.paragraph: The variables in the dual problem have useful economic interpretations. For example, consider the problem of mixing nuts studied in Example 5 of Section 9.2 and Example 6 of Section 9.3:

$$\begin{matrix} \text{Maximize} & f \left(x_{1} , x_{2}\right) & = & 2 x_{1} + 3 x_{2} & \\ \text{subject to} & x_{1} & \leq & 30 & ( \text{cashews} ) \\ & x_{2} & \leq & 20 & ( \text{filberts} ) \\ & x_{1} + 2 x_{2} & \leq & 54 & ( \text{peanuts} )\end{matrix} \text{and} x_{1} \geq 0 , x_{2} \geq 0.$$
Recall that $$x_{1}$$ is the number of boxes of the first mixture and $$x_{2}$$ is the number of boxes of the second mixture. Example 2 displayed the following dual problem:

$$\begin{matrix} \text{Minimize} & g \left(\right. y_{1} , y_{2} , y_{3} \left.\right) & = & 30 y_{1} + 20 y_{2} + 54 y_{3} \\ \text{subject to} & \text{y} _{ \text{1} } + y_{3} & \geq & 2 \\ & y_{2} + 2 y_{3} & \geq & 3\end{matrix} \text{and} y_{1} \geq 0 , y_{2} \geq 0 , y_{3} \geq 0.$$
If $$\mathbf{\overline{x}}$$ and $$\mathbf{\overline{y}}$$ are optimal solutions of these problems, then by the Duality Theorem, the maximum profit $$f(\mathbf{\overline{x}})$$ satisfies the equation
$$f \left(\right. \bar{x} \left.\right) = g \left(\right. \bar{y} \left.\right) = 30 \left(\overset{ˉ}{y}\right)_{1} + 20 \left(\overset{ˉ}{y}\right)_{2} + 54 \left(\overset{ˉ}{y}\right)_{3}$$

Suppose, for example, that the amount of cashews available was increased from $$30$$ pounds to $$30 + h$$ pounds. Then the profit would increase by $$h{\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{1}$$ . Likewise, if the amount of cashews was decreased by $$h$$ pounds, then the profit would decrease by $$h{\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{1}$$ . So $${\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{1}$$ represents the value (per pound) of increasing or decreasing the amount of cashews available. This is usually referred to as the marginal value of the cashews. Similarly, $${\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{2}$$ and $${\overset{ˉ}{y}}_{3}$$ are the marginal values of the filberts and peanuts, respectively. These values indicate how much the company might be willing to pay for additional supplies of the various nuts.2

Thus the marginal value of the cashews is $$\frac{1}{2}$$ , the marginal value of the filberts is $$0$$ , and the marginal value of the peanuts is $$\frac{3}{2}$$ .﻿

Note that the optimal production schedule $$\mathbf{\overline{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} 30 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix}$$ uses only $$12$$ of the $$20$$ pounds of filberts. (This corresponds to the slack variable $$x_{4}$$ for the filbert constraint inequality having value $$8$$ in the final tableau.) This means that not all the available filberts are used, so there is no increase in profit from increasing the number of filberts available. That is, their marginal value is zero.

section.heading: Linear Programming and Matrix Games
section.paragraph: Let $$A$$ be an $$m \times n$$ payoff matrix for a matrix game, as in Section 9.1, and assume at first that each entry in $$A$$ is positive. Let $$\mathbf{u}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ and $$\mathbf{v}$$ in $$\textbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ be the vectors whose coordinates are all equal to one, and consider the following linear programming problem $$P$$ and its dual $$P^{\ast}$$ . (Notice that the roles of $$\mathbf{x}$$ and $$\mathbf{y}$$ are reversed, with $$\mathbf{x}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{m}$$ and $$\mathbf{y}$$ in $$\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$$ .)

$$P : & \text{Maximize} & \mathbf{v}^{T} \mathbf{y} & & & P^{*} : & \text{Minimize} & \mathbf{u}^{T} \mathbf{x} & & & \text{subject} \text{to} & A \mathbf{y} & \leq & u & & \text{subject} \text{to} & A^{T} \mathbf{x} & \geq & v & & y & \geq & 0 & & & x & \geq & 0$$

The primal problem $$P$$ is feasible since $$\textbf{y} = \textbf{0}$$ satisfies the constraints. The dual problem $$P^{\ast}$$ is feasible since all the entries in $$A^{T}$$ are positive and $$\mathbf{v}$$ is a vector of $$1 \text{’s}$$ . By the Duality Theorem, there exist optimal solutions $$\mathbf{\overline{y}}$$ and $$\mathbf{\overline{x}}$$ such that $$\textbf{v}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{y}} = \textbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{x}}$$ . Set
$$\lambda = v^{T} \bar{y} = u^{T} \bar{x}$$

Since the entries in $$A$$ and $$\mathbf{u}$$ are positive, the inequality $$A\textbf{y} \leq \textbf{u}$$ has a nonzero solution $$\mathbf{y}$$ with $$\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{0}.$$ As a result, the $$\text{λ}$$ for the primal problem is positive. Let
$$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \bar{\mathbf{y}} / \lambda \text{and} \hat{\mathbf{x}} = \bar{\mathbf{x}} / \lambda$$

It can be shown (Exercise 29) that $$\mathbf{\hat{y}}$$ is the optimal mixed strategy for the column player $$C$$ and $$\mathbf{\hat{x}}$$ is the optimal mixed strategy for the row player $$R$$ . Furthermore, the value of the game is equal to $$1/ \text{λ}$$ .

Finally, if the payoff matrix $$A$$ has some entries that are not positive, add a fixed number, say $$k$$ , to each entry to make the entries all positive. This will not change the optimal mixed strategies for the two players, and it will add an amount $$k$$ to the value of the game. [See Exercise 33(b) in Section 9.1.]

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Solve the game whose payoff matrix is $$A = \left\lbrack \begin{array}{rrr} {- 2} & { 1} & { 2} \\ 3 & 2 & 0 \end{array} \right\rbrack$$ .
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: To produce a matrix $$B$$ with positive entries, add $$3$$ to each entry:
$$B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 4 & 5 \\ 6 & 5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$$
The optimal strategy for the column player $$C$$ is found by solving the linear programming problem

$$\begin{matrix} \text{Maximize} & y_{1} + y_{2} + y_{3} & & \\ \text{subject} \text{to} & y_{1} + 4 y_{2} + 5 y_{3} & \leq & 1 \\ & 6 y_{1} + 5 y_{2} + 3 y_{3} & \leq & 1\end{matrix} \text{and} y_{1} \geq 0 , y_{2} \geq 0 , y_{3} \geq 0.$$
Introduce slack variables $$y_{4}$$ and $$y_{5}$$ , let $$M$$ be the objective function, and construct the initial simplex tableau:

image.alt: A 3 by 7 augmented matrix is shown with columns 4 and 5 as slack variables.

example.paragraph: The three $$- 1$$ entries in the bottom row are equal, so any of columns 1 to 3 can be the first pivot column. Choose column 1 and check the ratios $$b_{i}/a_{i1}$$ . To bring variable $$y_{1}$$ into the solution, pivot on the $$6$$ in the second row.

image.alt: A 3 by 7 augmented matrix is shown.

example.paragraph: In the bottom row, the third entry is the most negative, so bring $$y_{3}$$ into the solution. The ratios $$b_{i}/a_{i3}$$ are $$\frac{5}{6}/\frac{9}{2} = \frac{5}{27}$$ and $$\frac{1}{6}/\frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{3} = \frac{9}{27}$$ . The first ratio is smaller, so pivot on the $$\frac{9}{2}$$ in the first row.

image.alt: A 3 by 7 augmented matrix is depicted.

example.paragraph: The optimal solution of the primal problem is

$$\left(\overset{-}{y}\right)_{1} = \frac{2}{27} , \left(\overset{-}{y}\right)_{2} = 0 , \left(\overset{-}{y}\right)_{3} = \frac{5}{27} , \text{with} \lambda = \left(\overset{-}{y}\right)_{1} + \left(\overset{-}{y}\right)_{2} + \left(\overset{-}{y}\right)_{3} = \frac{7}{27}$$
The corresponding optimal mixed strategy for $$C$$ is
$$\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \bar{\mathbf{y}} / \lambda= \left[\right. \frac{2}{7} 0 \frac{5}{7} \left]\right.$$
The optimal solution of the dual problem comes from the bottom entries under the slack variables

$$\left(\overset{ˉ}{x}\right)_{1} = \frac{1}{9} = \frac{3}{27} \text{and} \left(\overset{ˉ}{x}\right)_{2} = \frac{4}{27} , \text{with} \lambda = \left(\overset{ˉ}{x}\right)_{1} + \left(\overset{ˉ}{x}\right)_{2} = \frac{7}{27}$$
which shows that the optimal mixed strategy for $$R$$ is
$$\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \bar{\mathbf{x}} / \lambda = \left[\right. \frac{3}{7} \frac{4}{7} \left]\right.$$
The value of the game with payoff matrix $$B$$ is $$v = \frac{1}{ \text{λ} } = \frac{27}{7}$$ , so the value of the original matrix game $$A$$ is $$\frac{27}{7} - 3 = \frac{6}{7}$$ .

section.paragraph: Although matrix games are usually solved via linear programming, it is interesting that a linear programming problem can be reduced to a matrix game. If the programming problem has an optimal solution, then this solution is reflected in the solution of the matrix game. Suppose the problem is to maximize $$\textbf{c}^{T}\textbf{x}$$ subject to $$A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$$ and $$\textbf{x} \geq \textbf{0}$$ , where $$A$$ is $$m \times n$$ with $$m \leq n$$ . Let
$$M = \left[\right. 0 & A & - \mathbf{b} - A^{T} & 0 & c \mathbf{b}^{T} & - \mathbf{c}^{T} & 0 \left]\right. \text{and} \mathbf{s} = \left[\right. \bar{y} \bar{x} z \left]\right.$$

and suppose that $$M$$ represents a matrix game and $$\mathbf{s}$$ is an optimal column strategy for $$M$$ . The $$(n + m + 1) \times (n + m + 1)$$ matrix $$M$$ is skew-symmetric; that is, $$M^{T} = - M$$ . It can be shown that in this case the optimal row strategy equals the optimal column strategy, the value of the game is $$0$$ , and the maximum of the entries in the vector $$M\textbf{s}$$ is $$0$$ . Observe that

$$M \mathbf{s} = \left[\right. 0 & A & - \mathbf{b} - A^{T} & 0 & c \mathbf{b}^{T} & - \mathbf{c}^{T} & 0 \left]\right. \left[\right. \bar{y} \bar{x} z \left]\right. = \left[\right. A \bar{\mathbf{x}} - z \mathbf{b} - A^{T} \bar{\mathbf{y}} + z \mathbf{c} \mathbf{b}^{T} \bar{\mathbf{y}} - \mathbf{c}^{T} \bar{\mathbf{x}} \left]\right. \leq \left[\right. 0 0 0 \left]\right.$$

Thus $$A\mathbf{\overline{x}} \leq z\textbf{b}$$ , $$A^{T}\textbf{y} \geq z\textbf{c},$$ and $$\textbf{b}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{y}} \leq \textbf{c}^{T}\mathbf{\overline{x}}$$ . Since the column strategy $$\mathbf{s}$$ is a probability vector, $$z \geq 0$$ . It can be shown that if $$z > 0$$ , then $$\mathbf{\overline{x}}/z$$ is an optimal solution for the primal (maximization) problem for $$A\textbf{x} \leq \textbf{b}$$ , and $$\mathbf{\overline{y}}/z$$ is an optimal solution for the dual problem for $$A^{T}\textbf{y} \geq \textbf{c}$$ . Also, if $$z = 0,$$ then the primal and dual problems have no optimal solutions.

In conclusion, the simplex method is a powerful tool in solving linear programming problems. Because a fixed procedure is followed, it lends itself well to using a computer for the tedious calculations involved. The algorithm presented here is not optimal for a computer, but many computer programs implement variants of the simplex method, and some programs even seek integer solutions. New methods developed in recent years take shortcuts through the interior of the feasible region instead of going from extreme point to extreme point. They are somewhat faster in certain situations (typically involving thousands of variables and constraints), but the simplex method is still the approach most widely used.
